issues.description: The participant flow does not add up. The manuscript reports 468 at T1 and 450 at T4, implying 18 participants did not complete all waves, yet later states that only 16 were excluded for missing time points. It then reports a final N of 372 after excluding 78 poor-quality cases, which is consistent with 450 - 78 but not with the stated missing-time-point exclusion. The analytic tables later use N = 321 and N = 244, creating further unexplained discrepancies. These inconsistencies make it impossible to verify the actual analytic sample and attrition process.
issues.quote: "n = 468 nurses responded at time 1; n = 458 responded at time 2 (98% retention rate between T1 and T2); n = 454 responded at time 3 (98% retention rate between T2 and T3); and n = 450 responded at time 4 (98% retention rate between T3 and T4)." ... "Only participants who completed all four surveys (n = 16 people excluded due to missing time points) and whose responses passed a priori determined data quality checks (n = 78 people excluded for poor data quality) were included in the final sample." ... "This resulted in a final sample size of N = 372."

issues.description: Although the final sample is reported as N = 372, Table 1 and Table 2 use N = 321 and Table 3 uses N = 244. The manuscript does not adequately explain why 51 cases are absent from the primary mediation analyses or why 128 cases are absent from the moderated analyses. This is a substantial loss of data and may bias estimates if missingness is related to workload, acuity, distress, or incivility.
issues.quote: "This resulted in a final sample size of N = 372." ... "Note. N = 321." ... "Note. N = 244. The sample size was reduced due to missingness on the moderator variable."

issues.subcategory: moderator missingness handled by listwise deletion
issues.description: The patient-acuity moderator has substantial missingness, reducing the moderated analysis to N = 244, but the amount, pattern, and mechanism of missingness are not reported in the methods. The apparent complete-case/listwise deletion approach can bias moderation estimates, especially because missingness resulted partly from incorrect responses, suggesting systematic misunderstanding rather than random missingness.
issues.quote: "Finally, our perceived patient acuity measure had missing data. For missing cases, responses were either left blank (55% of missing values were due to no-response) or the value provided was outside of the expected numerical range (45% of missing values were due to an incorrect response)." ... "Note. N = 244. The sample size was reduced due to missingness on the moderator variable."

issues.subcategory: complete-case longitudinal analysis after induced monotone dropout
issues.description: Participants who missed one wave were not invited to subsequent waves, creating monotone attrition by design. The authors then included only complete cases. This can bias longitudinal estimates unless missingness is demonstrably MCAR/MAR and appropriately modeled. No FIML, multiple imputation, inverse-probability weighting, or sensitivity analyses are reported.
issues.quote: "Due to budgetary constraints, participants who did not respond to a measurement period were not invited for subsequent surveys (i.e., a participant who did not complete T2 survey was not sent the link for the T3 or T4 surveys)." ... "Only participants who completed all four surveys ... were included in the final sample."

issues.subcategory: data-quality exclusion counts do not sum
issues.description: The manuscript states that 78 people were excluded for poor data quality, but the listed reasons account for only 57 exclusions: 56 for inconsistent demographics and 1 for missing more than 50% of items. The remaining 21 exclusions are unexplained, raising concerns about undisclosed exclusion criteria or reporting error.
issues.quote: "whose responses passed a priori determined data quality checks (n = 78 people excluded for poor data quality)" ... "(a) demographic information was not consistent across measurement periods (n = 56 people failed to provide reasonably consistent responses to tenure, gender, and/or age); or (b) missing values exceeded 50% of the questions (n = 1)."

issues.description: The exclusion criterion of failing to provide "reasonably consistent" demographic responses is subjective and insufficiently operationalized. The manuscript does not define allowable variation in age or tenure, whether birthdays or tenure changes were permitted, how inconsistencies were adjudicated, or whether exclusions were blind to outcomes. This creates researcher degrees of freedom that can affect results.
issues.quote: "demographic information was not consistent across measurement periods (n = 56 people failed to provide reasonably consistent responses to tenure, gender, and/or age)"

issues.description: The advertised inclusion criteria required full-time nurses in high-stakes/critical care settings, but the final sample is described as including part-time nurses and only requiring more than one shift per week on average. This changes the target population and may affect exposure opportunity, workload, and generalizability.
issues.quote: "Information about inclusion criteria (working full time in a high-stakes/critical care setting as a nurse)" ... "All participants were currently employed as a nurse (part- or full-time), worked more than one shift a week, on average, and routinely worked with high severity/high-risk patients."

issues.description: Recruitment relied on flyers, personal networks, social media, and voluntary opt-in links. The sampling frame and denominator are unknown, so response rates and representativeness cannot be evaluated. Participants interested in incivility, stress, or wellness may have been especially likely to participate, threatening external validity and possibly inflating associations.
issues.quote: "Although the full population size that was sampled from is unknown" ... "Participants were recruited from various hospitals across the U.S. using three recruitment strategies." ... "we sent emails to nurses and other healthcare professionals in our personal networks" ... "we posted study information and recruitment materials online via personal social network accounts"

issues.description: Eligibility for being a nurse in a high-stakes setting appears to have been based on self-report through public recruitment links. Given monetary compensation and online recruitment, this creates risk of ineligible or fraudulent respondents. The reported data-quality checks do not verify licensure, unit type, or employment status.
issues.quote: "For all recruitment strategies, participants initiated the contact and study procedures by clicking on the study link or QR code that was listed in recruitment materials" ... "To help ensure that the participants were from healthcare contexts, we highlighted the nursing focus in the recruitment and consent information and directly asked participants if they met the inclusion criteria."

issues.description: The manuscript does not provide essential contextual information such as unit type, hospital type, state/region distribution, shift type, nurse role, patient load, recruitment channel counts, or clustering by hospital/department. These details are needed to evaluate generalizability, possible nesting, and exposure to high-acuity patients.
issues.quote: "Participants were recruited from various hospitals across the U.S. using three recruitment strategies." ... "All participants were currently employed as a nurse ... and routinely worked with high severity/high-risk patients."

issues.description: The analyses regress later outcomes on earlier predictors but do not appear to control for prior levels of the same outcome variables, despite measuring every construct at every wave. Without autoregressive controls, the reported longitudinal paths may reflect stable between-person differences, trait negative affectivity, chronic unit climate, or baseline burnout rather than within-person change over time.
issues.quote: "We tested this hypothesis by regressing negative emotions toward patients (T3) onto experienced patient incivility (T2)." ... "Time 3 negative emotions toward patients were positively related to Time 4 compassion fatigue" ... "Time 2 experienced patient incivility was indirectly related to Time 4 enacted incivility toward patients"

issues.description: Compassion fatigue and enacted incivility are both measured at T4, using the same survey and same past-week recall window. This prevents establishing temporal precedence for the path from compassion fatigue to enacted incivility and undermines the serial mediation claim that compassion fatigue leads to future enacted incivility.
issues.quote: "T4 Compassion Fatigue" ... "Enacted Incivility (T4)"

issues.subcategory: causal language unsupported by observational design
issues.description: The study is a nonexperimental, self-report panel design. Although temporal ordering improves over cross-sectional data, it does not establish causality or rule out confounding, reverse causation, or stable third variables. Claims that incivility "leads to," "impacts," or "drives" later behavior overstate the design.
issues.quote: "These findings suggest that repeated exposure to incivility leads to both poor wellbeing outcomes for the target of incivility and to future enacted incivility."

issues.description: The model does not adequately adjust for plausible confounders such as trait negative affectivity, baseline mental health, prior enacted incivility, unit civility climate, staffing ratios, shift type, patient volume, specialty, hospital, leadership, or patient population. These factors could cause both experienced incivility and negative emotions/fatigue/enacted incivility.
issues.quote: "T2 Work Hours" ... "T3 Work Hours"

issues.description: Participants were recruited from multiple hospitals and likely nested within departments/units and recruitment channels. Hospital or unit climate can strongly influence incivility, workload, acuity, and fatigue. The analyses do not report random effects, cluster-robust standard errors, intraclass correlations, or any accounting for nesting, which may bias standard errors and inflate Type I error.
issues.quote: "Participants were recruited from various hospitals across the U.S. using three recruitment strategies."

issues.subcategory: selective use of waves despite measuring all constructs repeatedly
issues.description: All variables were measured at every wave, but the focal model uses selected waves only: T2 incivility, T3 negative emotions, and T4 compassion fatigue/enacted incivility. Many alternative lag structures were possible, and no preregistration or sensitivity analyses using other wave combinations are reported. This creates substantial researcher degrees of freedom.
issues.quote: "To better understand the effect of the predictor variables on the criterion variable at the subsequent time point, we assessed each variable during each wave." ... "The subsequent waves were included for hypothesis testing"

issues.description: The analytic strategy describes general mediation/moderated-mediation procedures but omits key reproducibility details: whether variables were modeled as latent or observed in hypothesis tests, estimator used for main regressions, centering of predictors/moderators, treatment of ordinal Likert scales, handling of missing data, covariance structure, inclusion/exclusion of controls, and exact model syntax.
issues.quote: "Next, we followed procedures described by Edwards and Lambert (2007), Hayes (2015, 2017), Preacher et al. (2007), and Selig and Preacher (2009) to estimate direct and indirect effects at each stage of the simple and moderated mediation models."

issues.description: For the serial mediation in Hypothesis 4, the indirect effect should include all component paths in the serial chain from experienced incivility to negative emotions to compassion fatigue to enacted incivility. The manuscript states that it was estimated by multiplying "the first and last stages" and labels this as a × d, which is incomplete and inconsistent with standard serial mediation notation.
issues.quote: "Here, the indirect effect was estimated by multiplying the first and last stages in the serial mediation process (a × d)."

issues.description: The reported Hypothesis 4 indirect-effect statistics are internally inconsistent. In the text, B = .06 with SE = .04 would not yield p < .01, whereas Table 2 reports the same effect with SE = .02. The table also reports t = 2.58, which does not equal .06/.02. These inconsistencies call the statistical inference for the central hypothesis into question.
issues.quote: "Time 2 experienced patient incivility was indirectly related to Time 4 enacted incivility toward patients (B = .06, SE = .04, p < .01, 95% CI [0.02, 0.10])." ... "Customer Incivility  Negative Emotions  Compassion Fatigue  Enacted Incivility | .06** | .02 | 2.58"

issues.description: Several reported test statistics do not match the displayed coefficients and standard errors after ordinary rounding. For example, B = .26 and SE = .06 imply approximately 4.33, not t = 4.50. Such discrepancies suggest rounding, transcription, or model-reporting errors that reduce confidence in the reported results.
issues.quote: "T2 Customer Incivility |  |  |  | .26*** | .06 | 4.50"

issues.subcategory: supplemental regression coefficients conflict with primary table
issues.description: The supplemental regression of enacted incivility on experienced incivility, negative emotions, and compassion fatigue reports coefficients that differ substantially from the primary mediation table, apparently for the same outcome and predictors. The manuscript does not explain whether a different sample, estimator, scaling, or model was used.
issues.quote: "we regressed enacted incivility on predictors from this stage--experienced incivility (B = -.03, SE = .04, p = .40), negative emotions (B = .23, SE = .04, p < .001), and compassion fatigue (B = .23, SE = .04, p < .001)." ... "T2 Customer Incivility ... -.07 | .05 | -1.14" ... "T3 Negative Emotions ... .28** | .10 | 2.89" ... "T4 Compassion Fatigue ... .57*** | .17 | 3.35"

issues.description: The manuscript states that the compassion-fatigue coefficient is nearly six times the negative-emotions coefficient. In Table 2, compassion fatigue is .57 and negative emotions is .28, about twice as large, not six times. This mischaracterizes the results and supports an overstatement about compassion fatigue being the stronger driver.
issues.quote: "the last step of the simple mediation reflects a parameter estimate for compassion fatigue that is nearly six times that of negative emotions."

issues.subcategory: relative importance analysis overinterpreted under multicollinearity
issues.description: The predictors in the enacted-incivility model are extremely highly correlated, especially compassion fatigue and enacted incivility, and likely negative emotions and compassion fatigue. Relative importance metrics can be unstable and sample-dependent under such multicollinearity. The manuscript does not report confidence intervals, robustness checks, or VIFs, yet interprets percentages as meaningful variance contributions.
issues.quote: "The results revealed compassion fatigue, negative emotion, and experienced incivility accounted for 45.1%, 30.8%, and 24.1% of the variance in enacted incivility, respectively."

issues.subcategory: poor discriminant validity among key constructs
issues.description: The bivariate correlations among focal constructs are extremely high, including r = .94 between T4 compassion fatigue and T4 enacted incivility, raising serious concerns that the constructs are not empirically distinct or are dominated by common method/response style. The CFA claim is insufficient without factor correlations, alternative model statistics, or tests showing separability of highly correlated latent factors.
issues.quote: "T4 Compassion Fatigue | 2.73 | 1.22 | ... .96" ... "T4 Enacted Incivility | 2.77 | 1.21 | ... .94 | .91"

issues.description: Negative emotions and compassion fatigue overlap conceptually and in item content. Negative emotions include frustration, irritability, anger, and resentment, while the manuscript defines compassion fatigue as including irritability and aggression. This overlap can inflate the negative-emotions-to-compassion-fatigue path and make the mediation partly tautological.
issues.quote: "The scale items consisted of four negative emotions: (a) frustration, (b) irritability, (c) anger, (d) resentment." ... "The burnout component of compassion fatigue relates to feelings of hopelessness, anxiety, irritability, aggression, cynicism"

issues.subcategory: weekly measurement of chronic compassion fatigue
issues.description: Compassion fatigue is described as progressive and cumulative, but measured with a past-week frequency frame at each wave. The manuscript does not provide validation that the Compassion Fatigue-Short Scale can validly capture week-to-week fluctuations or that a one-week lag is theoretically appropriate for this chronic construct.
issues.quote: "Combined, both components of compassion fatigue are progressive and cumulative" ... "For all scales, participants were prompted to respond about their experiences over the past week."

issues.description: Patient acuity is operationalized as a single self-reported percentage of patients considered "severe." This departs from established acuity systems and does not capture intensity of care, staffing ratios, number of patients, or gradations of severity. A single item also prevents reliability assessment.
issues.quote: "we measure the respondents’ perceptions of patient acuity across all patients they attended to within the last work week by asking them to estimate a percentage of their patients that were ‘severe.’"

issues.description: The acuity item asks participants across different departments to anchor their responses to potentially different scales, including ESI, CRIB, SOIS, and even patient-reported outcome tools. These instruments have different scoring systems, populations, and meanings, so the resulting percentage "severe" is not comparable across respondents.
issues.quote: "Some example scales include: the Emergency Severity Index (ESI), the Clinical Risk Index for Babies (CRIB), the Severity of Illness Scale (SOIS), or other patient-reported outcome (PRO) assessment tools"

issues.subcategory: actual invalid acuity responses indicate item misunderstanding
issues.description: Nearly half of the missing acuity values resulted from responses outside the expected numerical range. This directly contradicts the pilot claim that respondents understood the item and suggests that the operationalization was confusing. The resulting missingness and measurement error threaten the validity of the moderation test.
issues.quote: "45% of missing values were due to an incorrect response"

issues.description: The acuity percentage lacks a denominator. A nurse seeing 2 patients and a nurse seeing 40 patients can report the same percentage severe, but the precision and workload implications are very different. The authors acknowledge not collecting the number of patients seen, which weakens the acuity construct and its interpretation as workload.
issues.quote: "we did not ask them to report on the specific assessment used, number of patients seen in that week, or the number of patients that were actually classified as severe within their assessment tool."

issues.subcategory: perceived acuity confounded with affect and incivility perceptions
issues.description: The moderator is a subjective perception measured by the same respondent at the same wave as experienced incivility. Negative affect, burnout, or stressful interactions could influence both perceived acuity and reported incivility, making it difficult to interpret patient acuity as an exogenous contextual moderator.
issues.quote: "Within this study, we look at perceptions of patient acuity across all patients seen within a given work week"

issues.subcategory: source and target mismatch across measures
issues.description: Experienced incivility is measured as behavior from patients or patients' family/friends, negative emotions are measured only toward patients, and enacted incivility is measured toward patients or family members. This creates a mismatch in the source/target of constructs and complicates interpretation of the proposed patient-directed mechanism.
issues.quote: "patients or patient family members/friends" ... "How often do you feel the following emotions towards patients" ... "patients/patient family members"

issues.subcategory: enacted incivility items may capture clinical judgment or triage rather than incivility
issues.description: Some enacted-incivility items are problematic in healthcare. Doubting a patient's or family member's judgment may be clinically appropriate, and paying limited attention may reflect triage or workload rather than rude intent. Without contextualization or external validation, these items may not validly capture nurse incivility.
issues.quote: "Doubted one or more patient’s/patient family members’ judgment on a matter over which they had responsibility," "Paid little attention to one or more patient’s/patient family members’ statements or showed little interest in their opinions"

issues.subcategory: shortened scales selected by factor loadings
issues.description: The manuscript reports selecting the highest-loading items to shorten scales. Selecting items primarily by factor loadings can narrow construct coverage and inflate internal consistency, especially for multifaceted constructs such as incivility and compassion fatigue. Part-whole correlations in a small pilot do not establish full construct validity of the shortened/adapted scales.
issues.quote: "For each scale, the highest loading items were chosen from reported factor analytic data to maintain a reasonable survey length and achieve internal consistency reliability"

issues.subcategory: self-report of socially undesirable enacted incivility
issues.description: Enacted incivility toward patients is socially undesirable and professionally consequential, making self-reports vulnerable to underreporting, impression management, and common-method bias. No patient, peer, supervisor, behavioral, or incident-report data are used to validate the outcome.
issues.quote: "This study is a four-wave panel longitudinal design that will include administration of self-report online questionnaires" ... "Thinking about your interactions with patients during the past week, how often have you…?"

issues.description: All focal constructs are self-reported by the same person, and the final mediator and outcome are measured in the same survey. Temporal separation of some variables does not remove same-source response styles, negative affectivity, social desirability, or consistency motifs. The very high correlations among constructs suggest common-method or general distress variance may be substantial.
issues.quote: "our data were collected using self-report questionnaires" ... "we temporally separated the measurement of variables across four measurement periods"

issues.subcategory: frequency measures not adjusted for exposure opportunity
issues.description: Experienced and enacted incivility are measured as weekly frequency ratings, but the analyses do not adequately adjust for patient volume, number of shifts, number of interactions, or hours of direct patient contact. Nurses with more patient encounters have more opportunities both to experience and enact incivility, potentially confounding the associations.
issues.quote: "Thinking about your experiences at work during the past week, how often have you been in a situation" ... "Thinking about your interactions with patients during the past week, how often have you…?"

issues.description: The confirmatory factor analysis is inadequately reported. The chi-square statistic is missing its label, alternative model fit statistics are not shown, the wave(s) used are unclear, factor loadings and factor correlations are omitted, and RMSEA = .08 is only borderline despite being called acceptable. This is especially problematic given the extremely high observed correlations among constructs.
issues.quote: "The fit of the four-factor model was acceptable (269) = 862.05, RMSEA = .08, CFI = .99, TLI = .99) and fit the data better than alternative models with fewer factors."

issues.subcategory: unregistered supplemental analyses and researcher degrees of freedom
issues.description: The manuscript reports supplemental analyses addressing unhypothesized moderation and relative importance. There is no preregistration, analysis plan, or correction for the multiple possible models generated by measuring all variables at all waves. This raises concerns about undisclosed exploratory decisions and selective reporting.
issues.quote: "We conducted a series of supplemental analyses to 1) address unhypothesized moderation effects and 2) investigate the relationship between compassion fatigue and enacted incivility."

issues.description: No a priori power analysis, minimum detectable effect, or precision justification is provided for the mediation, serial mediation, or moderated mediation models. This is important because moderated mediation and interactions require large samples, and the moderator analysis drops to N = 244.
issues.quote: "We tested our hypotheses using data collected across four waves separated by one-week lags." ... "Note. N = 244. The sample size was reduced due to missingness on the moderator variable."

issues.description: The authors state that Hypothesis 3 predicted employees with higher acuity would report higher negative emotions, but the simple slopes reported test the association between incivility and negative emotions at levels of acuity. They do not test whether high-acuity employees have higher mean negative emotions; the acuity main effect is reported as nonsignificant in Table 3.
issues.quote: "Hypothesis 3 also predicted that the conditional relationship would be such that employees reporting higher perceived patient acuity would also report higher negative emotions. Simple slope analysis estimates at low ... medium ... and high ... levels of the moderator revealed support for Hypothesis 3."

issues.description: The supplemental analyses explicitly report that the conditional indirect effect and index of moderated mediation were nonsignificant. Nevertheless, the discussion and practice implications imply that high acuity places nurses at greatest risk for fatigue and ultimately enacted incivility. That conclusion is not supported by the nonsignificant moderated mediation.
issues.quote: "the slopes at low ... medium ... and high levels ... were all non-significant" ... "the IMM was non-significant" ... "employees experiencing incivility from patients and who have a high perceived patient acuity load are at the highest risk of experiencing increased negative affect and fatigue and, ultimately, engaging in incivility."

issues.description: The abstract says patient acuity exacerbates "these detrimental relationships," but the reported significant moderation applies only to the path from experienced incivility to negative emotions. The conditional indirect effects through compassion fatigue to enacted incivility are nonsignificant. This makes the abstract misleading.
issues.quote: "perceived patient acuity can exacerbate these detrimental relationships"

issues.subcategory: mediation described as partial without clear support
issues.description: The discussion describes a partial mediation process, but for the enacted-incivility outcome the direct effect of experienced incivility appears nonsignificant after mediators in Table 2. The manuscript should distinguish the significant direct path to compassion fatigue from the nonsignificant direct path to enacted incivility.
issues.quote: "Our results support a partial mediation process" ... "T2 Customer Incivility ... Enacted Incivility (T4) ... -.07 | .05 | -1.14"

issues.description: The manuscript claims to use social learning theory, but the described mechanism is the stressor-emotion model: environmental stressors leading to negative emotions and counterproductive behavior. Social learning theory concerns observation, modeling, reinforcement, and learned consequences, none of which are measured or theorized in the hypotheses. This conceptual mismatch weakens the theoretical rationale.
issues.quote: "To understand how incivility experiences from customers may be impacting employee affect and behavior over time, we utilize social learning theory (Bandura, 1977)." ... "Applied to enacted incivility, the general premise of the model suggests that enacted incivility occurs due to a sequence of events where environmental stressors at work lead to enacted incivility through appraisal, perceptions of the stressor, and negative emotions (Spector & Fox, 2005)."

issues.description: The compassion fatigue section says the study examines coworker incivility, contradicting the stated focus on patient/customer incivility. This may be a wording error, but it creates ambiguity about the hypothesized stressor.
issues.quote: "Within the current study, we look specifically at the relationship between experiencing coworker incivility and experiencing a caregiving specific form of job burnout, compassion fatigue."

issues.subcategory: overgeneralization from specialized nurse-patient context to customer service broadly
issues.description: The sample consists of nurses in high-stakes healthcare settings, a context involving ethical duties of care, clinical authority asymmetries, family involvement, team-based care, and high emotional stakes. Claims about customers and service industries broadly should be more limited, especially given the self-selected and overwhelmingly female nursing sample.
issues.quote: "This adds to the generalizability of prior customer incivility research to further support that experiencing incivility from customers – even when the customers are patients, a population of people you have dedicated your career to care for – is associated with detrimental employee and customer outcomes over time."

issues.subcategory: patient-nurse relationship treated as customer-employee despite important conceptual differences
issues.description: The manuscript acknowledges that patient-nurse relationships are more complex than ordinary customer-employee interactions but nonetheless frames patients as customers throughout. Patient vulnerability, clinical responsibility, legal/ethical duties, and family involvement may change the meaning of both incivility and enactment, limiting construct equivalence with customer incivility.
issues.quote: "We view the patient-nurse relationship as a specialized form of customer-employee relationship. However, it is important to understand that this relationship includes care provision and care coordination, which is more complex and dynamic than some other employee-customer relationships."

issues.description: The pilot studies are used to justify scale adaptations and a new acuity item, but details are sparse. The quantitative pilot was small, recruited through MTurk, and apparently relied on self-reported nurse status. The manuscript does not report pilot demographics, verification procedures, factor loadings, reliability estimates, or item-level results needed to evaluate adaptation validity.
issues.quote: "The quantitative pilot consisted of n = 50 nurses who worked in high-stakes settings and were recruited from MTurk."

issues.description: The authors justify one-week lags by citing prior studies on counterproductive behavior and asserting that effects would not meaningfully differ with longer lags. The manuscript provides no empirical lag sensitivity tests, and the focal processes include immediate emotions and potentially chronic compassion fatigue, which may operate on different timescales.
issues.quote: "Previous studies have shown that lags spanning this length of time are sufficient for observing emergence of such counterproductive behaviors as incivility and that the observed effects will not meaningfully differ from studies featuring longer periods of time between waves"
